text:
I need a sales page for my meal delivery service. I'm a registered dietitian, and I run a weekly delivery of cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes in our metro area.

Facts:
- 10 meals a week cost $129, delivered every Sunday. A trial week costs $59.
- Every meal has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less, and I plan each menu myself.
- We have 88 active customers. 37 of them have been with us more than six months.
- 14 customers shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. 10 went down, 3 stayed about the same, and 1 went up. The average drop was 0.6 points.
- I don't track whether customers changed their medication during that time.
- About 1 in 5 people who try a trial week sign up for the full plan.

I want the page to say our meals will lower your A1C. Around 400 words.

Before I draft, there's one decision for you and a few questions.

**The A1C claim**

"Our meals will lower your A1C" promises a result to every reader. Your numbers support something smaller.

- **What you have:** 14 of your 88 customers shared their results. For 10 of them, A1C went down after three months. The average drop was 0.6 points. For 1 person it went up.
- **What a skeptical reader, or a regulator, would say:**
  - People with good results are more likely to share them.
  - You don't know who changed medication.
  - One customer's A1C rose, so "will" is already untrue for someone.

  Your data can't answer these, and a reader with diabetes has probably heard big promises before. A health claim about food that you can't fully back also creates legal and professional risk for you as a registered dietitian.
- **What the facts do support:** "Of 14 customers who shared their A1C with me before starting and three months later, 10 saw it go down, by 0.6 points on average. I don't track medication changes, so I can't say how much of that was the meals. I can say every meal is under 45 g of carbohydrate and planned by a registered dietitian."

  This version is stronger than it looks. Stating the limits openly makes the 10 of 14 believable. It also sits well with your best evidence, which is retention: 37 customers have stayed more than six months.

I'd recommend the second version, but it's your call. Which do you want?

**Questions**

1. **What can a customer cancel, pause or skip, and with how much notice?** For a $129 weekly plan, this is the first thing a reader looks for.
2. **What does a typical week of meals look like?** Two or three real dishes would help a lot. Can you handle allergies or preferences like vegetarian or no pork? "Diabetic food is bland" is the objection you most need to answer.
3. **How do you work alongside customers' doctors and medications?** For example, do you share nutrition info they can bring to appointments, or check in with them? Someone on insulin or a sulfonylurea will want to know.
4. **Your name, credentials and business name.** Include years in practice and any certification like CDCES. Also tell me which metro area or zip codes you deliver to.
5. **How do people sign up, and by what day for Sunday delivery?**
6. **Should the page mention the trial conversion rate?** About 1 in 5 trial customers sign up for the full plan. Readers won't see that number, so I'd leave it off unless you know why the other four don't continue. If the reason is cost or a delivery limit, it may be worth addressing on the page.

Answer what you can, and I'll write the roughly 400-word page from there. I won't make up anything you skip.

Fair point, go with the second version. I can't promise anyone's A1C will drop, and the meals don't replace their doctor's advice.

1. No contract. They can skip a week or cancel any time.
2. Each week they can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices, and the menu repeats every 4 weeks. I don't have specific dishes or allergy info to give you right now.
3. I don't work with their doctors directly. I can do a 15-minute phone call with each person before they start.
4. Lena Ortiz, RD. The business is Steady Plate. We deliver within 25 miles of downtown. I don't know what else to add on credentials beyond RD.
5. They start a trial week from the order button. Orders close Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery.
6. I don't know why the others don't continue, so leave it off.

I've written it as the second version, with the A1C results stated alongside their limits. It's about 400 words, and I used only the facts you gave me.

# Steady Plate

## Cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes, planned by a registered dietitian

Knowing what to eat with type 2 diabetes is one job. Cooking it twice a day, every day, is another. Steady Plate does the second one for you.

Every Sunday we deliver 10 cooked lunches and dinners to your door. Every meal has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less, and I plan every menu myself.

— Lena Ortiz, RD

## What customers have seen

Fourteen customers shared their A1C results with me, once from before they started and again three months later. For 10 of them, A1C went down, by an average of 0.6 points. Three stayed about the same, and one went up.

That's a small group. I don't track whether anyone changed their medication during that time, so I can't tell you how much of the change came from the meals. I can't promise your A1C will drop, and Steady Plate doesn't replace your doctor's advice.

I can promise you'll know what's on your plate: cooked meals, each with 45 grams of carbohydrate or less, planned by a registered dietitian.

Right now, 88 people get our meals each week. Thirty-seven of them have been with us for more than six months.

## How it works

**Talk to me first.** Before your first delivery, you get a 15-minute phone call with me. Ask me anything about the meals before you start.

**Make the week yours.** You can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices. The menu runs on a four-week cycle.

**Get it on Sunday.** We deliver within 25 miles of downtown. Orders close Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery.

**Stay only as long as it helps.** There's no contract. Skip a week or cancel at any time.

## Pricing

**Trial week:** $59

**Full plan:** $129 a week for 10 meals, which is $12.90 a meal

## Start with one week

You don't have to commit to anything to find out whether Steady Plate works for you. Order a trial week by Thursday at noon and your meals arrive on Sunday. If it helps, stay. If it doesn't, cancel. There's no contract.

**[Start your trial week]**

A few things to check before it goes live:

- **"25 miles of downtown":** if your city's name would make this clearer for readers, swap it in.
- **The trial week:** the page doesn't say how many meals it includes or whether it rolls into the full plan, because I didn't know. If it does roll over, say so next to the button. Readers who find out after being charged $129 will feel misled.
- **Sample dishes:** when you have two or three, add them under "Make the week yours." They're the best answer to people worrying that meals for diabetes will be bland.
